read: full: abstract, sections 1-5, limitations (p.1-9), Appendix A (construction details, including A.7 expert validation, p.13-14); the result tables (p.7-8) and Appendix B fine-grained results and checkpoint lists (p.14-23) skimmed.
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2606.03660v2 [cs.AI], 3 June 2026 (p.1 margin stamp); no venue shown. The benchmark's name is ChemCoTBench-V2 (p.1).
what_it_is: ChemCoTBench-V2 is a chemistry benchmark of 5,620 samples in 18 reporting tasks (31 fine-grained) across molecular understanding, molecule editing, molecular optimisation and reaction prediction, drawn from public databases and normalised with RDKit (p.1, p.3, p.14). Models must answer in expert-refined templates that expose named intermediate steps with structured outputs (p.3). Three signals are reported separately: final-answer correctness, template adherence, and step-wise verifier correctness. The step checks are deterministic: intrinsic RDKit rules (Type-I), agreement with a verified reference trace for closed-answer tasks (Type-II), and oracle constraints for optimisation; there is no LLM judge (p.1, p.4-5). The reference traces are written by GPT-5.4 and Claude-Opus-4.7 conditioned on the ground-truth answer and kept only if they pass the checks (p.3). Three chemists' step labels on 300 traces agree with the verifier on 87.4% of steps (kappa 0.74) (p.14).
domain: chemistry (molecular understanding, molecule editing, molecular optimisation, reaction prediction); not engineering
size: 5,620 evaluation samples, 18 reporting tasks covering 31 fine-grained tasks (p.1, p.14); 8 frontier LLMs evaluated (p.5).
source_of_items: public chemistry databases and corpora: PubChem, ChEMBL and ZINC for molecular understanding; atom-mapped USPTO-derived Schneider 50K reactions for editing; matched molecular pairs with property oracles for optimisation; reaction, retrosynthesis, condition and yield pools for reaction prediction (p.3, p.14). Templates are induced from natural model CoT by an LLM and pruned by chemistry experts (p.3).
instances: static: sampled once from public databases, filtered and canonicalised (p.3, p.14). Condition-ranking labels are shuffled and answer-leaking metadata removed (p.3).
has_gold_traces: yes, for closed-answer tasks: step-level reference traces generated by GPT-5.4 and Claude-Opus-4.7 from the input, the ground-truth answer and the template, retained only if they pass Layer 1, Layer 2 and Type-I checks, with conflicts inspected manually or excluded (p.3). The authors call them 'verified benchmark-state trajectories rather than unique human reasoning processes' (p.9). Optimisation tasks use oracle constraints instead (p.5).
evaluation: step-level or process, deterministic: Layer 1 final-answer metrics by task (exact match, MAE, Tanimoto, top-1 accuracy, success rate); Layer 2 template adherence and field consistency; Layer 3 step-wise checks, namely Type-I intrinsic RDKit predicates (SMILES validity, SMARTS matching, ring counts, heavy-atom arithmetic, conservation), Type-II all-match against the reference trace, and an oracle-verified optimisation score (p.4-5). Evaluated over structured template fields, not free-form CoT sentences (p.3, p.9).
human_validation: Templates: chemistry experts remove fields that are not meaningful, stable or deterministically verifiable (p.3). Verifier: 3 expert chemists independently labelled each step of 300 randomly sampled step-level traces as correct, incorrect or ambiguous, with majority adjudication; the deterministic verifier agreed with the adjudicated label on 87.4% of step judgments (Cohen's kappa 0.74), against human-human agreement of 90.1% (kappa 0.79). Disagreements concentrate in tasks with several valid paths (optimisation, condition ranking, retrosynthesis) (A.7, p.14).
contamination_measures: none: the items come from public databases (p.14). Answer-leaking metadata is stripped and condition-ranking labels are shuffled against shortcuts (p.3), which is not a contamination measure.

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate; the May paper does not cite it, and it does not cite EngTrace. It is the closest outside precedent for EngTrace's verification design: deterministic checks of intermediate states against reference states instead of an LLM judge, reported separately from the final answer, with the verifier validated against expert step labels (p.4-5, p.14).

suggested_wording: In chemistry, ChemCoTBench-V2 (Guo et al., 2026) makes models expose intermediate steps in fixed templates and checks them with deterministic RDKit rules and model-generated reference traces rather than an LLM judge, agreeing with three chemists on 87.4% of step judgments (kappa 0.74); its items are drawn from public databases rather than generated.
facts_to_cite: 5,620 samples in 18 reporting tasks across molecular understanding, molecule editing, molecular optimisation and reaction prediction (p.1, p.3)
Items drawn from public chemistry databases (PubChem, ChEMBL, ZINC, USPTO-derived reactions) and normalised with RDKit (p.3, p.14)
Models must fill expert-refined templates that expose named intermediate steps with structured outputs (p.3)
Three signals reported separately: final-answer correctness, template adherence and step-wise verifier correctness (p.1, p.4)
Step checks are deterministic (RDKit rules, agreement with reference states, oracle constraints) with no LLM judge (p.1, p.4-5)
Reference traces are generated by GPT-5.4 and Claude-Opus-4.7 conditioned on the ground-truth answer and kept only if they pass the checks (p.3)
Verifier against 3 expert chemists on 300 step-level traces: 87.4% agreement, Cohen's kappa 0.74; human-human 90.1%, kappa 0.79 (p.14)
Final answers can be right while steps fail: SMILES equivalence reaches 86.9% outcome accuracy but 29.9% step-level all-match (p.7)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: deterministic step-level verification against reference intermediate states instead of an LLM judge (p.4-5), which is the design of EngTrace's milestone and arithmetic checks; outcome and process reported separately; the finding that correct answers hide invalid steps (p.7); validation of the verifier against several experts' step labels with chance-corrected agreement (p.14), which parallels EngTrace's X1 study. Lacks: the engineering domain; generated instances (static, from public databases, contamination unaddressed); gold traces computed by code (its reference traces are LLM-written and answer-conditioned, then filtered, p.3, p.9); evaluation of free-form reasoning (models must fill a fixed template, and only its structured fields are checked, p.3, p.9). What EngTrace adds beyond it: engineering problems generated from templates with a private seed, gold traces derived from the template code, and checks that read values from the model's own free-form trace rather than from a prescribed template (per the state brief's E3 and E4).
notes: (1) Priority is a judgement: the paper is chemistry, not engineering, and a reviewer of an engineering benchmark might not name it. I rate it 'must' because the revised text will present deterministic checks of intermediate values, validated against experts, as EngTrace's method, and this paper does both outside math. It belongs in the process-supervision and judge-validity paragraph (or the physical-sciences paragraph), not the engineering one. The facts above are high confidence. (2) Naming: this is V2 of ChemCoTBench; the web search note lists 'ChemCoTBench' (v1) under chemistry, so keep the two apart in the bibliography. (3) Its reference traces are generated with the answer in hand, which the authors acknowledge (p.9), a contrast with EngTrace's gold traces computed forward by template code.
